I've never played a Persona game, and never really played JRPGs either to be honest. The fanciest I've ever gotten with these types of games is honestly Pokemon.

This game is insane, and I'm loving it. The plot sucks you in, the characters usually make you laugh(there's a couple of moments that make me cringe, but hey so does everything with characters so whatever), and the gameplay is incredibly addicting.

A lot of people reviewing are pushing this game as people who are playing it for nostalgia reasons, or because they love JRPGs and this is the cream of the crop. Let me say as a total newbie to the scene, Persona is just as inviting for new players as it is the long-time players.

I 100% fully recommend this game to anyone who has even the slightest of interest in RPGs.

2008: Persona 4 came out on the PS2. I dropped 85 hours into it, and it ended up being my favorite PS2 game of all time.

2012: Persona 4 Golden came out on PS Vita. I bought it at launch and finished it twice (including the Platinum), dropping another 120 hours into it. It ended up being my favorite PS Vita game of all time.

2020: Persona 4 Golden surprise launched on Steam. I was 45 hours into a playthrough of Persona 5 Royal, but put it on indefinite hold to play this instead. I'm 6 hours in... you probably know how this story ends by now.

Buy it. Great port, great game.

Thank you Atlus for making this playable on PC as it was impossible before. And thank you everyone for buying this and showing Atlus we want their games on here.

Can't wait to finish this game, having a blast so far.

EDIT: I finished this game, and I loved it. Honestly it can bring you to tears, strike your heart, and leave you wanting more. I absolutely loved this game, and I hope Atlus brings more of their games on here, if they do I'll pre-order them in a heartbeat!!!

Just to preface the review: I’m aware that this might get lost in the sea of reviews currently written for the game, but really, I don’t care. If this helps sway even a single person to get this game, then it’ll be worth it. Plus, after 100 hours of pure joy and entertainment, the very least I can do is add my own voice to the over 14k people who have already voiced their opinion. This game, aside from being a lot of fun, has become one of my favourites of all time. I was reminded of very important life lessons while playing, and that’s not something many games can accomplish.

If you are a fan of JRPGs, or even remotely interested in this game, and want my final verdict without reading everything, here goes, in no uncertain terms:

[b]Get this game.[/b]

-----------

Disclaimer before I start: [b]this is spoiler free.[/b] Any major plot point mentioned here is already readily available in the steam store page description or trailer - I’m using those as a guide for what’s a spoiler. So don’t worry!

The game store page describes it as “A coming of age story that sets the protagonist and his friends on a journey kickstarted by a chain of serial murders.” I can safely say that is a better description than I will ever be able to come up with. From that, here’s what I can tell you about the story:

- “...by a chain of serial murders”. It’s a murder mystery, and a REALLY good one. The story as a whole is incredible. It offers an extremely good balance of slice of life things and seriousness, and you actually look forward to both of those moments. Sprinkled along the game, you have full on anime cutscenes, which are freaking amazing, and while used sparingly, they were very well employed to build both tense moments and lighthearted moments.

- “A coming of age story...” Now there’s an interesting term. Coming of age for who? Not just the protagonist. And herein lies the magic behind the game, and one of its strongest bases (I honestly cannot overstate this enough): [b]the relationships.[/b] Throughout the game you, a new kid in town, meet a vast and amazing cast of characters. Some, you’re going to hate from the get go (sorry Chie; Ai). Some you’ll love (Rise best character and I’ll fight anyone who says otherwise). But I guarantee you: throughout the game, even if your opinion on them doesn’t change for better or worse (and there’s a good chance it will), you will notice a change in the characters, mainly because of its Social Link system.

Coming off that point, I have to praise the game even further on one specific aspect: [b]it has one of the best casts of main characters I have ever had the pleasure to see in a game.[/b] Your friends feel exactly like that: friends. Despite being fundamentally very different, every person in the group has such an amazing chemistry with each other that everything involving the group feels… natural. There are scenes that will make you cry from laughter, and others that will make your heart race as you see the events unfold on your screen. The characters aren’t perfect either. Quite the contrary: they’re flawed. They’re human, with all the quirks that come with that. One of them, for example, often goes into laughing fits at the weirdest moments - and as a person who often does the same, I couldn’t help but smile and relate to it whenever it happened. 

[b]The core gameplay loop can be separated into two bits: dungeons and slice of life stuff.[/b] The game works with a calendar system: days go by just like in real life. Every day, you get 2 “slots” to do things - after school/afternoon and evening. Some days, story may occupy one, or both, of those slots. When you have the free time, you have free reign to do whatever you want with your days: you start at school, often answer a question posed by the teacher, and then all bets are off. You can talk to friends (some are only available on certain days), you can engage in various activities like fishing, you can study, heck, you can even go back in dungeons to explore them again. The game continues this way, until things happen and… you are locked into the story sequence that leads you to your next dungeon.

Whenever you unlock a dungeon, you are given a time limit to do it, and can engage it anytime within the limit. The gameplay while [b]dungeon-crawling is… monotonous at best.[/b] Coming from persona 5, I was severely disappointed with this aspect of the game. The dungeons are expansive, with multiple floors, but they are also semi procedurally generated, with little to no variation within each one. Every floor consists of corridors with square rooms every once in a while, unless it’s a special floor. Littered throughout the floor, you’ll find enemies - Shadows. A lot of them. Each dungeon took me 2-3 hours (as I’m cursed with the need to explore everything before moving on) and they were not fun. Even the combat, which is good - turn based with a unique element of creating new personas - is not enough to help that front. Eventually I resorted to watching tv shows while I mindlessly took care of the dungeons.

And another important detail: [b]the game takes a while to get going.[/b] You’re thrown into the mystery within the first hour, but if I recall correctly, I played for 2 or 3 hours until I was allowed actually do things in the game aside from reading. This is an issue with a lot of JRPGs, and to some people (like myself), it’s not an issue at all, but it’s still worth mentioning. This is a story to be experienced slowly, and not rushed through, and the beginning alone makes that very clear.

The artstyle honestly is one of my favourites, and [b]the game has an incredible soundtrack.[/b] Man oh man, the soundtrack. It is one of the strongest I’ve ever seen in a game. I’d put it up there, in my personal rankings, with the likes of nier automata, world ends with you, and of course, Persona 5. At times hauntingly beautiful, and at times downright unnerving, I promise you one thing: you will often catch yourself grasping at your headphones (if you play with them), just appreciating how much bliss is coming through your ears. I honestly can not WAIT to play the rhythm game, because with this amazing soundtrack involved, it’s going to be one hell of an experience. I’d link some videos here so you could hear it for yourself, but… I think you might be better off experiencing it in game.

I do have another very important aspect to mention, which is the [b]importance of this port[/b]. From the SMT mainline games to Persona, its spin offs/sequels, Catherine and even other, lesser known series and games, ATLUS has a lot of FANTASTIC games under its wings - all of them on platforms other than the PC. Nobody expected (as far as I’m aware anyway) a Persona game to come to PC, and while this was most likely SEGA’s doing, it really brings me joy to see the game, at the time of writing, with over 14k reviews, and sitting at “Overwhelmingly Positive”. Maybe, just maybe, with how successful this port has been, as well as the Catherine one, we’ll get the other games too. Now that this is on PC… anything is possible.

There is a LOT more to say. My original review was twice as long, at least, before I found out steam had a set number of letters that I could use in a review. If you want to know more, I’m always down to talk. All in all, I truly believe this game is [b]almost a masterpiece.[/b] What attracts me most in games is, by far, a good story, and words are not enough to describe how well the game delivers on that front. You’re going to enjoy every bit spent with the crew, and chances are it’ll be one of those bittersweet endings, where you’re happy you experienced the story, but sad that it’s over. I know that’s how it was for me.

Thank you for reading, and if you do jump in... I sincerely hope you enjoy the ride. Words are simply not enough to express how much I did.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
I have always wanted to play a [b]Persona[/b] game. So, when [b]Atlus[/b] brought [b]Persona 4[/b] to [b]Steam[/b], I was excited beyond belief that I could finally have the opportunity to play one! I was treated with a fun combat system, an engaging story, and wonderfully crafted characters that made me emotional in the end. There is a lot to do, but it’s up to you on what you want to experience in [b]Inaba[/b]. The game will play out in a murder mystery style of gameplay, as its main focus. Also, you don’t need to play any of the other [b]Persona[/b] games, you can jump straight into this one.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]A fantastic story that proves emotional with well-written characters.
[*]Combat feels very engaging and fun with offensive and defensive spells/attacks.
[*]Lots of activities to do in [b]Inaba[/b].
[*]The soundtrack is really catchy.
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]To get the best ending, you have to max out [b]Marie’s Social Link[/b], and she is not a well-written character.
[*]Investigations can get quite confusing, as you have to go around and ask certain [b]NPCs[/b] who are only available on certain days.
[*]The 3D human character models are the original PS2 ones, and they haven’t aged very well.
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story takes place in the year 2011. The protagonist is being sent to a town called [b]Inaba[/b] because his parents are working overseas. He moves in with his uncle [b]Ryotaro Dojima[/b] and his younger cousin [b]Nanako[/b]. While at his new high school, he becomes friends with [b]Chie Satonaka[/b], [b]Yukiko Amagi[/b], and [b]Yosuke Hanamura[/b]. The peaceful town is dealing with some bizarre murder cases and it seems to be related to [b]The Midnight Channel[/b], So one rainy night, he decided to look at the TV and saw a strange figure, then he decided to enter the screen only to find himself in another dimension. The protagonist also has a dream where he is taught how to summon a [b]Persona[/b], however, he also has a special ability called the [b]Wild Card[/b] which gives him the ability to summon multiple [b]Personas[/b].

Now, that’s only scratching the surface of what [b]Persona 4[/b] has to offer in terms of story. It’s well written, full of mystery and suspense that’s going to keep you invested. However, the story does have some moments where it’s not serious and has humor. There are quite a few characters that are really memorable in the game, and they each have their own unique traits. My two personal favorites had to be [b]Yosuke[/b], as he was clumsy as well awkward, and [b]Naoto Shirogane[/b], who is a detective, while being a mysterious kind of character.

Now, some characters, however, are not as good as the main cast and a good example is, [b]Marie[/b], she is a character that is exclusive to [b]Persona 4 Golden[/b]. The reason I bring her up is that to get the best ending in the game, you will have to max her [b]Social Link[/b]. [b]Marie[/b] has no memory of who she is or why she even exists, so it’s your job to try and get her to remember things. The problem with her, is that her role is to basically not like you or anyone and comes off as aggressive, while being one dimensional.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
[b]Persona 4[/b] is a [b]turn based-RPG[/b], and you will be fighting enemies known as [b]Shadows[/b]. These enemies will have certain elemental strengths and weaknesses that you can use to take them out more easily. The party members that you will get will have a certain element that is associated with them, like having wind, ice, or fire just to name a few. You will be using your [b]Personas[/b] in combat to cast spells and you can do a normal attack with your characters. At the end of each battle, you will be rewarded with experience points to level up your character. At the end of a dungeon, you will fight a boss; these bosses aren’t really a challenge and are mostly sponges, but the later ones can get a little tricky. Once you are done with that dungeon, you can revisit to fight an optional boss to get some extra goodies. Combat is rather fun and it’s really smooth, definitely something that has aged very well. Also, one of the enemies you fight is literally an army tank, so that should pique some interest. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2289932509 

After you are finished with some battles, you may get an event known as [b]Shuffle Time[/b]. This event will show you a list of cards, and you can only choose one. These cards can give you bonuses like extra money or EXP. You can also get your hands on [b]Suit of Swords[/b]. These will give you [b]Skill Cards[/b] which will teach a skill for your [b]Persona[/b]. The power will depend on the value of the card. You can also get a card that has a negative effect; however, you can pick more cards if you choose to pick it.

The only issue I really came across the gameplay was when it came to the [b]Investigations[/b]. There will be certain points in the game where you will have to find some information on certain people before entering a dungeon. The main issue here is that some NPCs will only appear on certain days. Especially on the fifth investigation, where you have to ask certain people in a specific order.

[h3]Past Times/Social Links[/h3]
When school is done or it’s during the day, you will have the chance to hang out with your friends. They will have their very own [b]Social Link[/b] with which they can learn new moves while hanging out with you. Certain characters have a corresponding [b]Arcana Tarot Card[/b]; these can be used to get EXP bonuses for other [b]Personas[/b] that you can use. If you get one of your party members’ [b]Social Link[/b] maxed, their [b]Persona[/b] will evolve and become stronger.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
The port of [b]Persona 4[/b] is really solid. I experienced no issues whatsoever; everything worked fine. It runs at 60 FPS, and it may feel weird to someone who played the original on the [b]PS2[/b], as that one runs at 30FPS. All the enemies and [b]Personas[/b] are fully animated and look amazing; they have aged very well. The 3D human models have not and are very hard to look at, with animations not looking good either. Now, the 2D sprites on the characters, are well done, the art style used for them has aged well. I tested it with an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, and16 GB of RAM storage. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2289932555 

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
Man, I love the soundtrack of [b]Persona 4 Golden[/b]. The battle theme was great. Boss battles also had a nice ring to them. There was never a song that I did not like listening to, each felt and sounded different. Choosing my favorite was really hard. However, I will give it out to [b]Snowflakes[/b], as it takes place in the wintertime and I just loved listening to it. The song was sung by [b]Shihoko Hirata[/b].

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
[b]Persona 4 Golden[/b] is an interesting experience. I have never played an RPG quite like this and every second was amazing. When it was all over, I just wanted to play more of it to experience everything all over again. The game has a ton of replay value as there is a so much to do in it. As a result, a single playthrough is not enough, as [b]Persona 4[/b] has a lot offer. Honestly, this was an experience worth remembering, and anyone that wants to start out with a [b]Persona[/b] game or RPGs in general need look no further than this one. Also, For the current price of 23.99 CDN, with 50-70 hours of content; well worth it at full price.

Frankly...I don't know what I could say about Persona 4 Golden that hasn't been echoed by so many folk during the game's time on the Vita and the short time it's been on Steam since last month, if the hundreds of reviews are anything to go off of. Persona 4 Golden is a great time. It's a great game with an interesting story and satisfying gameplay.

Although, since I had just finished Persona 5 Royal mere weeks before Persona 4 Golden came to Steam and had a chance to finally play it, I had a lot of things I really needed to readjust to. So if you've played Persona 5, the original or Royal, and are thinking of going back to Persona 4 Golden to see what this game was about, keep in mind that you may have a bit of a tough time re-adjusting to certain aspects of gameplay.

I'll actually start off things I disliked about the gameplay itself, which - excuse me if it'll sound like I'm just too spoiled by Persona 5 and Persona 5 Royal. But nevertheless, these are things that bothered me throughout my entire playthrough.

[h1]Things I didn't like:[/h1]
[b]- Dungeons[/b]
They felt...boring. The dungeons in this game were very very boring for me, as most of them were pretty much randomly generated sets of hallways covered with fog, teeming with shadows but also treasure. There have been countless times where going through the dungeons I genuinely felt like I was going to fall asleep. Thematically they are [b]really good,[/b] I love the themes for dungeons that are presented here. I just wish navigating them was more fun than going through hallways, opening doors and grabbing treasure until you find the next staircase.

[b]- Engaging shadows[/b]
This is what I had to readjust to the most after playing Persona 5 Royal and that game was very fresh on my mind. Engaging shadows feels incredibly clunky. I had this same issue with Persona 3 Portable but the same issue persists here too. I didn't like how shadows could see you from any angle you approach them, making a stealthy approach impossible unless you draw the Avoid Encounters card during Shuffle Time. I got the hang of it by the time I entered the third dungeon of the game, as it's about making your move during the second the shadow notices you and the "!" appears. But even after figuring that out, I still feel it was very clunky.

[b]- Lack of encouragement for most social links[/b]
Again - another thing I'm kinda spoiled by thanks to Persona 5 (and Royal). There's not really much incentive to do social links in this game. Maxing out links with your party seems like a no-brainer - they get a bunch of awesome benefits as you level them, useful skills as you go through, the works. But maxing out non-party social links feels unsatisfying. If you don't care about earning additional money or raising your social stats, most of them feel pretty pointless. Of course 2 of them are required for story progression if you want to go forth to the [i]true[/i] ending, but aside from them - there's not much point to social links aside from missing out on Arcana Bursts and money/social stats.

[b][u]- THE PC PORT.[/u][/b]
I REALLY REALLY DON'T LIKE THE PC PORT. It has its positives - I was very surprised and happy to find out my PS4 controller worked right out of the box without having to emulate it as an X360 pad, but holy CRAP. There's missing sound effects, there's random game stutters, particularly often when prompted for an All Out Attack, [b]AND THE DAMN THING CRASHES OFTEN![/b] These are issues I [i]really[/i] hope Atlus will fix in the future. So depending on when you're reading this - this might not even be relevant anymore.

That's about it for the things I disliked about Persona 4 Golden. Keep in mind - this was essentially my first playthrough of the game. Now what about the things that I really liked about it?

[h1]Things I liked/loved:[/h1]
[b]- The story and characters[/b]
I still prefer Persona 5's story because it's a lot more relatable to me personally, but I really enjoyed Persona 4 Golden's story. Really! The murder mystery alongside a quiet town aesthetic, while a bit cliche, was very interesting to follow along. I honestly enjoyed how it continued to throw you for a loop, and some parts of the story actively made me jump out of my seat and go "woah what the hell?!". Of course it did have its low-points, but there's a lot of quotable lines from this game's story and it's overall very interesting to follow along. It knows how to pace itself, when the proper time to crack a joke, the works. Also screw Teddie. I found Teddie very annoying all the way through.

[b]- The soundtrack[/b]
PERSONA 4'S MUSIC IS GOOD. REALLY GOOD. I prefer the PS2 opening of the game to Golden, but I won't deny at all that this game's soundtrack is a serious bop. The song that plays right before dungeons, known as "Studio Backlot", is seriously my favorite song from this game. It's just so good.

[b]- The gameplay loop[/b]
Yeah, I mentioned that I thought the dungeons were boring and that engaging shadows was clunky, but to be perfectly honest - the gameplay loop [i]itself[/i] is very good. A good variety of meaningful mechanics and enough time to learn about, adjust to and then abuse the hell out of your enemies. The gameplay, despite being jank in some aspects, does often feel incredibly rewarding.

Do I recommend Persona 4 Golden? As if you thought I was going to say "no". Persona 4 Golden is a great time to be had. And while it is a bit jank and the graphics haven't exactly aged gracefully, seeing as Persona 4 was originally a PlayStation 2 game made in 2008, neither of those facts change that this game is phenomenal. And you should totally give it a shot. There's at least 60 hours worth of fulfilling content in this, if not [i]way more.[/i] I just hope they touch up the PC port in the future so it quits crashing and stuttering, as well as fix the missing sound effects issue.

Persona 4 Golden (P4G) was originally released in 2012 for the PlayStation Vita and is the “extension” or director’s cut to Persona 4 (2008). The PC version was unexpectedly announced on the PC Gamer Show’s E3 2020 presentation and many flocked to the Steam store to purchase the game. I never heard of the Persona series before and purchased the game immediately to see why P4G is highly regarded as one of the best games ever created. The story follows the main character residing at a small, rural Japanese town with his uncle and cousin while unexplained killings, kidnappings, and supernatural elements taking place. Does this mystery visual novel and JRPG fused game has your interests? 

P4G is first and foremost, an JRPG game, but what makes the game special is the strong, character developments among major and minor characters via Social Links. Social Links are represented of the protagonist’s relationships among characters. This usually starts from acquaintances, associates, or classmates and evolves to closest friends, allies, or romantic relationships. Social Links are also associated to the characters’ Arcana such as Chariot, Priestess, Lovers, Emperor, and many more. Social Links, in some way, can be associated to a character’s personality. An example would be a character who constantly flirts with the protagonist is associated to the Lovers’ Arcana. The advantages of Social Links are ranged from further EXP points from Persona fusions to the specific Arcana, awakening a character’s potential and character arc. Most characters are well-written and has great character developments. A few characters are alright but doesn’t hinder much of the overall story. The other gameplay mechanic is time management. The player has the options to hang around with friends and acquaintances to increase Social Links rankings, work on a part-time job, study, read books, and other various attributes. It's more of a balancing act, but the most important aspect is to establish and enhance social relationships. The protagonist's Social Stats are also important too which allows the player to open or resume Social Links, part-time jobs, or allow to pick certain dialogue options. 

The voice acting performances in the game is astonishing and perhaps one of the voice casting ensembles ever assemble in a video game. For the English dub version, there’s Johnny Yong Bosch, Troy Baker, Laura Bailey, Yuri Lowenthal, Karen Strassman, and so much more. The performances are top notch to the point where I honestly would give them an Oscar for best actors and actresses. It’s a rare gem of which I prefer the English version over the native Japanese voiceovers (the Japanese cast is also excellent, but it all comes down to personal preference or acting performances) because my gosh, the English voice acting is A+++. Additionally, the original soundtrack for the game is catchy, memorable, and sometimes emotional. 

The core fundamental of Personas is quite hard to explain, but to simplify things, a “Persona” is centralized on various folklores and folktales, mythologies, polytheistic religions, and Christian symbolism around the world. Common examples are Japanese and Chinese mythologies, Norse mythologies, Hindu gods and goddesses, and many others I couldn't fill out. Each Persona provides various attributes to turn the battle into your favor. The supernatural elements in the game takes place in the TV world and the protagonist and his friends arise to take the challenge. I am not going to go further details on the plot, but the story experience and characters’ evolution on working as a team really pays off. 

I brought P4G around E3 2020 amidst the COVID pandemic and an uncertain future. The game has a lot of wholesome moments, and the acting performances feels genuine as if the voice cast had a lot of fun. The game feels like a Japanese Scooby-Doo mystery with mature, thematic elements blended very well. I finish the game for the first time around late August 2020 and replayed the game for the second time via Steam Deck in May 2022. The experiences in both desktop and Steam Deck are great. P4G was my personal Game of the Year 2020 (based upon the games I played in the year, not on the game’s release date) and I am glad I experienced the game. P4G is an essential purchase. My highest recommendation.

This is without question the best game I have played in the last decade and [u] easily one of the best games I have played in my life. [/u] The writing below is as much a love letter to the game as it is a review. Even if this gets lost in the shuffle of other glowing reviews, I want to do my part to show my adoration for this masterpiece. 

[h1] Introduction [/h1]

I never thought I’d be writing this review, much less playing a game like Persona 4 Golden in the first place. I don’t play JRPGs, I don’t consume visual novels, I don’t engage with the anime aesthetic. I’d heard about the Persona series a handful of times, but it was purely on a whim that I bought Persona 4 Golden. 

I fell in love with the game within the first few minutes. Give me the perfect ingredients — soundtrack, atmosphere, characters, and plot, and suddenly I’m hooked. Suddenly, I’m staying up until 3 a.m. every night exploring each corner of the world, talking to every NPC, and keeping track of in-game events in writing. Below I’ll detail several components of the game without any spoilers or specific giveaways. 

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The game, and consequently the story, is delivered through a calendar system. Each day in-game is spent participating in the gameplay loop. When one day ends, you go on to the next one and have different options. The day matters — For example, you go to school on weekdays, and some NPCs are only available during certain days of the week. Similarly, weather and time of day also matter — For example, many quest NPCs won’t be available when it’s raining and some activities, like jobs, are only available during the night. You go through the gameplay loop each day; this lasts for roughly one calendar year. 

I’d split the core gameplay loop into three parts — Free-roam, Visual Novel, and Dungeon Crawling. 

[b] Free-roam [/b]

A significant portion of the game is spent exploring various hubs in town. Yes, there’s still an overarching narrative that you’re following along, but there are moments in between for you to seek out and accomplish different things. You can interact with NPCs, spend time with companions, visit shops, collect items, complete quests, and more. This part of the gameplay loop is your chance to interact with the world.

[b] Visual Novel [/b]

My favorite part of the core gameplay loop. These are your deep character interactions, cutscenes, and story exposition. This is the meat of the game. If you don’t like reading/listening to lengthy sections of dialogue, then I would not recommend this game to you because this is arguably the most important piece of the experience. I use the term “Visual Novel” for a reason! 

Spending time with your companions and other residents of the town is a major component of the game as well. In doing so, you get really neat character development, storytelling, and upgrades to a gameplay mechanic called “Social Links” that affect combat and a couple other things. 

During Visual Novel moments, you get opportunities to make dialogue choices in response to the other characters. Some responses are just for flavor, some affect how much other characters like you, and some even affect the plot in significant ways. In true RPG fashion, you’ll feel like your choices matter over the course of the game. 

[b] Dungeon Crawling [/b]

As you progress through the story, you unlock mandatory dungeons that must be beaten in order to avoid a game over. Thus, combat is central to the gameplay loop. In these dungeons you traverse floor after floor, fighting or evading enemies and collecting loot along the way until you reach a final boss. Your standard RPG fare. 

Combat itself is your run-of-the-mill turn-based battling with some unique twists. I won’t spoil what those twists are, but there are enough aspects to the combat that keeps it interesting. If you’re playing on a harder difficulty, you are compelled to grind for experience, money, and items, as that is the only way you can prepare for boss fights. Depending on the kind of gamer you are, the grind could be a good or bad thing. I personally found myself lowering the difficulty so I could focus on the story of the dungeon rather than the challenging fights.

[h1] Highlights of the Game [/h1]

If you’re still with me to this point then that means a lot to me. I can write endlessly about this subject, but I want to make sure that this review is actually functional in informing you about the game. To that end, I’m going to highlight the most noteworthy parts of the game from my perspective. 

[b] Plot [/b]

The story of Persona 4 Golden can be best described as a rollercoaster. Constant twists, turns, ups, downs, and surprises. You will smile, laugh, cry, and feel sick to your stomach. Sometimes all of those feelings, multiple times, in one play session. Considering that the plot has to do with a mystery, that is a very good thing.

I was so emotionally and cognitively invested in this story that I would go about my day constantly thinking about what was going on. “Why did ‘x’ happen? Who did it? What does ‘y’ mean?” An embarrassingly high amount of my mental bandwidth was consumed by the going ons of this game even outside of playtime. I simply had to solve the mystery! Even if it meant losing sleep over it. 

[b] Characters [/b]

Perhaps the brightest highlight and selling point of this game. The characters you meet and interact with are what make everything worth it. They give purpose and meaning to the narrative. They give you, the player, opportunities to explore your own self through them. Their ideals, opinions, struggles, and reflections feel so brutally honest that you can’t help but feel something in response. There are countless examples of tear-jerking speeches, inspiring monologues, and heartwarming camaraderie in the cast. You’ll find yourself coming back to particular characters, spending time with them, learning about them, and even helping them with their personal challenges. 

There was not a single character in this game that I disliked. Your companions, friends, love interests, enemies, and antagonists were all written expertly and beautifully. 

[b] Soundtrack [/b]

Music cannot be discounted. After all, it lends a great amount of atmosphere to the whole experience of Persona 4 Golden. Between the solo piano movements, funk bops, and symphonic rock and JPop tracks, there’s a lot of variety to be had here. I found myself falling in love with genres of music I had never explored before. Hell, I’d linger in certain areas and sections of the world merely to hear a particular track on loop. Each song had its place and carried meaning with it. Emotional scenes were complemented well by moving score while the battle music was great at conveying the right feeling — whether hope or dread. 

Despite there being repeat tracks, I never once got sick of them. I grew to expect certain tracks at times, but they were always welcome. My favorite aspect to the soundtrack, though, was the remixing and editing of previously heard songs. A fast-paced rock song from a battle scene would later become a slow, dirge-like horn solo during a different scene. I always appreciated whenever I’d hear familiar notes delivered differently. 

[h1] Closing [/h1]

If you read through all of this tired man’s musings, then I thank you. I hope you got something of value from this review, even if only an itch to play (or replay) the game. If you’re anything like me — hungry for good storytelling, lovable characters, and deep, emotional experiences — then I guarantee that Persona 4 Golden is worth trying. You won’t be disappointed. If you have any questions or comments, please don’t hesitate to leave a reply or reach out to me.

Take care and thank you for your time.

Over the past couple of years, I have had little interest for games that can tell a great story. Instead, I would be forcing myself to play games such as the new COD and countless multiplayer focused games (you can see by my hours on the multiplayer games I play compared to single player games xD) . While these games allowed me to invest time into gaining new items to customise my character and they provided free updates to expand the base games. I still was 'making' myself play these games out of habit rather than 'wanting' to play these games out of free will.

Before Persona 4, I had never really considered playing a JRPG, as I assumed that it was just not my thing. The only game I have played that's close to this genre is Pokemon, but I wouldn't consider it as a 'hardcore JRPG'. However, due to the popularity of persona 5 royal and Joker being added to Smash Bros, I was curious about trying the Persona franchise. I looked up a couple of review videos and since I do not have a Playstation and therefore cannot play Persona 5, I thought screw it and went and bought 'Persona 4 Golden' as I was bored and was not invested in a particular game. I was pleasantly surprised.

The story in this game is awesome. The basic premise is that your character moves to a small town of Inaba which seems normal and boring at first. Then a bunch of murders occur and you and your friends are the only ones who can solve them. It sounds basic but I assure you, there are many twists and turns in the story that keep you questioning everyone you have met around town. Because any of them could be the murderer. You discover you have a 'persona' which is basically the 'other you' which you use to fight in many difficult and engaging battles. The battle system seems complicated at first but the game does help you understand at a basic level. This was way different from what I as used to as Pokemon held your hand at various points in the game (especially the new games!). However, I saw this as a breath of fresh air, as I enjoyed the challenge. I eventually became well accustomed to the battle system, but the battles still require you to plan ahead and provided a challenge, even on normal mode!

I also was not expecting the sheer depth of each character that you meet. Obviously, there are some characters I preferred over others, but each character has their own insecurities that they try to hide and as you get to know them, you help them overcome their fears and allow them to accept their true self. This allows you to create more personas and your team mates can upgrade their personas the more you get to know them. So there is a benefit of socialising with everyone around town. The chemistry that you build with your team mates and the people around you was another thing I was not expecting, you end up caring for the characters that you meet and that's how you know the writing in a game is on point. Another thing I would like to mention is the humour in this game! There were some really funny moments especially from one of the characters called Teddie (my favourite character) that generally make you laugh to yourself. I haven't had that from a game for a long time (last game that made me laugh was probably GTA V).

Finally, I heard the soundtracks in Persona games were good, but I was not expecting Persona 4's to be outstanding. I was wrong. The battle music and the music around town are great, as they clearly represent the emotion and feeling of the current place you are at. When you are walking around town there is relaxing music that changes depending on the season. In battle the music gets amped up and this is how I would relate it to Pokemon being the battle music is always good. Furthermore, there is voice acting for the main characters you meet. For the most part the voice acting is awesome however some characters have better than others. That does not stop this game from being the great game it is though!

To summarise, this game balances action with story telling fantastically. I have not had an experience with a game like this in a long time. The graphics are dated yes, but that did not affect the gameplay or how the story was told. At this point I have not written an in depth review for any game I own, but I feel that this game truly deserves it. If you have never played a JRPG before, do not be put off this game, as it is a gem. I would even recommend getting this game when it is not on sale, as the amount of content and replayability is worth the price tag in my opinion. I really hope Persona 5 comes to PC and with Strikers on Steam, this is a good sign. Do not sleep on this game! I would give this game a 9/10, as I am a believer that no game is perfect no matter how good.

Don't let my 18 hours on steam deceive you into how many hours I've sunk into this game across the years. From the OG PS2 version to the ps vita release of Golden, and now finally to the PC. I've played this game so many times, guides to test questions/Social Links are useless to me. I am the guide. All in all i would say I probably have around 600+ hours or so would be a good guesstimate for how much I've played p4. SO, with that in mind, here's my review:

Story: It should be stated that each persona game is a standalone title. You don't need to play the previous ones in order to play newer ones, but if you have played them before, you can enjoy various easter eggs that are scattered about. Anyways, onto P4...the start of the game can be a little slow (Especially if you're not used to JRPG's) but once you get through the first couple hours of playtime the game picks up speed and doesn't stop. From start to finish, it will leave you wanting more. The pacing is done extremely well too, giving you just enough information to keep you coming back, while withholding just enough to keep you on the edge of your seat. By the time the end of the game comes around, you'll become horribly depressed that it ended so soon. (Even though most playthroughs take on average 40-80 hours depending on your style of play)

Gameplay: Simplified, the game typically follows an order like this ----story stuff happens unlocking a new dungeon----game gives you X amount of days to complete the dungeon----you spend these days completing the dungeon, as well as doing multiple things around town, such as building social links with characters, working various jobs to make money, improving your personal attributes, and much more-----Once X amount of days have passed, and assuming you've cleared the dungeon, repeat from step 1.

Once you get into a dungeon you'll have to navigate yourself through a randomly generated floor until you find the staircase that will take you to the next level. Along the way you'll have enemies scattered about, as well as treasure chests and other things. Each dungeon has its own determined amount of floors, with various events that occur as you make your way to the final level. Some will be puzzles, others will be battles, or it may just be a cut scene. The boss, like usual, will typically await you on the final floor. Once beaten, you've cleared the dungeon.

Combat: The combat in persona is fairly simple. Its a standard turn based system that lets you control all allies in battle (Max of 4) or you can have the CPU control them for you (Not recommended. Just trust me.) Attacks are split between magical and physical, with both options having a wide range of unique skills to choose from. Most enemies will have a certain type of attack they are weak to, and if discovered can lead to something which the games calls "One More", knocking down the enemy and letting you immediately take another turn with the character that hit the weakness. Keep in mind this is true in reverse though, if the enemy hits your weakness, they will act again. 

Characters: The cast of P4 is one that you'll remember for a lifetime. Every character, both main and supporting, is unique in some way and has their own personal goals that they're trying to achieve. While you might find one character annoying, you may also fall head over heels for another.  As the MC, you can choose to spend time with both your party members, and other NPC's around town to help deepen your bond with them and progress their story, ultimately assisting them in accomplishing their goals.  This game also includes a romance system, allowing you to date any one (or all, for those aiming to become a Chad. Just don't get caught ;) ) of your female party members, as well as a few other NPC's. Depending on who, or if, you romance a character, it can change their dialogue towards you in certain scenes, as well as unlock special scenes between the two of you.

Final thoughts: I'm a huge persona nerd with P4 being my personal favorite so far. If you're even remotely thinking about picking this game up and trying it, just do it. $20 is BEYOND a good deal for this masterpiece, and if it happens to be on sale then IMO it should be a no-brainer. It has all the elements a good game should have and knocks every aspect out of the park.  10/10.

I originally bought P5R, played through it, and didn't really like it. The story dragged on, the combat wasn't the best, the calendar didn't let me relax, and the dungeons could be an absolute headache.

So, one day I was watching a game conference and they revealed Persona 4 Golden for Steam. Having almost beat P5R, I wasn't sure if I should get it. I decided 'screw it, why not'. Because it was on Steam and not the PS5 it made it easier to load up, my computer has a bad graphics card and I think it could handle it, and the premise seemed cool.

I decided to buy the deluxe version since it was only like $25.

I have currently played this game for 212 hours, and have yet to beat it. None of this time was spent unwillingly. The problems I had with P5R are either nonexistent or irrelevant.

Persona 4 Golden for Steam is my favorite game of all time.

The time I've spent so far in the game will be likely doubled with subsequent playthroughs, and I know I'll play it again solely on how fantastic the game is.

$25 is thievery for this game, I would be willing to pay $125 easy for it.

It feels great waking around the world, both in controls and the absurdly good music, the story is engaging at its peaks and actually tolerable at its valleys, the combat is interesting and surprisingly open, the substories are some of the best in gaming history, leveling with behemoths like Yakuza, and the world is condensed and focused.

I doubt that those who've gotten this far in the review are really on the fence about the game, but in the unlikely chance you are, please do buy this game. I wholeheartedly recommend it, and struggle to think of a better use of your money past bare essentials.

Before this game, I played the following Atlus games: Catherine Classic, Metaphor: ReFantazio, and Persona 3 Reload. Notice how visually stunning and fancy all these games are? But despite the artistic excellence of all these games, I can dare say with confidence that Persona 4 Golden is the greatest of all Atlus games I played, primarily due to its excellence in writing.

I had always been obsessed with writing in creative works, and this game provided me with a conclusive proof that writing is indeed the most important element in any form of creative work involving storytelling. You can invest all your resources into stunning visuals, but it would take only a few years, or even a few months until your 'stunning' visuals are outmatched by another brand-new work in the market. However, an excellent writing can easily make your work into a timeless classic, that can still compete in the market down the road against generations of new works. Persona 4 Golden is the first game that proved to me that this principle can apply to not only literature but also video games, which typically have far shorter lifespan in the market.

Persona 4 Golden's main theme is rigorous pursuit of truth in rejection of willful ignorance, convenient lies, and self-centered fantasies, all of which are metaphorically represented by the fog surrounding the protagonist and his village. This theme manifests not only in the main storyline, but also in the side stories of characters who are not directly involved with the protagonist's investigation activity. Every one of them faces a situation where they are either stuck in or tempted to accept false narratives that either they themselves created or other people forced onto them.

Our main cast, the Investigation Team members, also go through this process a bit more extensively and experience identity crisis where they are forced to question their own senses of identity. The protagonist is also no exception. Although he is more or less a typical blank sheet character designed for player immersion, he is [u]repeatedly[/u] presented with big choices he has to make, whether to resort to willful ignorance, or to keep pursuing truth despite discomfort. Given how post-truth politics flourishes in this modern day and age and constantly wrecks every sense of long-term stability for the sake of short-term gratification, Persona 4 Golden's lesson can't be more relevant to us.

What's more, interestingly, this game's true final boss explicitly states that his actions were motivated and legitimized by the vast majority of humanity that prefers willful ignorance to verifiable truth, which makes this whole game into a cautionary tale against mob rule. It's academically interesting how a Japanese video game translated the sophisticated theories of ancient Greek philosophers into a child-friendly argument for the need of constant vigilance against democracy decaying into mob rule, which is exactly the reason why prominent ancient Greek philosophers openly opposed the very idea of democracy during their time despite its merits. In that sense, the true final boss's underlings can also be interpreted as the perfect examples of how willful ignorance and compromised integrity can make you evil, whether you meant it or not. Seriously, it's unbelievable how this game was created two decades ago in Japan and points its finger with bone-chilling accuracy at the sociocultural problems rampaging our modern day society both worldwide and in USA.

Truly a timeless classic that cannot be ever more relevant to us now, Persona 4 Golden also highlights how unwavering pursuit of truth enables you to build stronger connection with your neighbors and friends. This is done by juxtaposing how the protagonist's Investigation Team shares ironclad friendship and how those who chose to indulge in willful ignorance and compromised integrity are always walking on eggshells, and sometimes destroy the genuine connections they were lucky to have with their own hands. This message is even more clear when you consider how even the Investigation Team's friendship gets challenged if the protagonist chooses willful ignorance over uncomfortable truth when given the choice. The more you look into this game's narrative structure, the more lessons you find on how rigorous pursuit of truth leads to robust connections, lasting fulfillment, and genuine happiness. The fact that this is done in simple vocabularies typical of Shonen manga is arguably the epitome of the literary adage: "Show, don't tell." Who would have imagined that Shonen manga vocabs are all it would take to teach the lessons on truth that countless philosophers wrote books about over centuries? The more you know of this game, the more impressive it gets.

I'm fully convinced after a playthrough that this game, Persona 4 Golden, is indeed one of the greatest, if not the greatest, Atlus games. I have not played Persona 5 yet, so this might be too early to make a conclusive statement, but I did hear repeatedly from others that Persona 4 is the greatest of the Persona franchise despite its outdated graphics. Now I know why. I have no objection to that evaluation. At the very least, this game's writing was way better than that of Metaphor: ReFantazio, which is the latest Atlus game in the market; it was visually impressive, but the story had very noticeable plot holes here and there and sometimes did not make sense at all by my standard. I have very little experience with the (Shin) Megami Tensei series of (mostly) jRPG titles by ATLUS. I first learned of the series after the huge success of Persona 3 about 11 years ago, which is in itself part of the sub-series of games with a different story and gameplay focus. I did play Persona 3 FES around the same time. I loved the unique blend of social simulation and turn based jRPG dungeon crawling and the overall dark horror mood of the story got me through a huge chunk of the game, but in the end I’ve never finished it. Same happened with the original Persona 4, which I’ve tried a few years later – I liked the premise and the gameplay, but playing on PS2 with its loading speeds get to me in the end and I dropped it, hoping that later the game will be ported to other platforms where its problems will be alleviated somewhat.

Persona 4 Golden was such a port… which I did miss because I never owned a PS Vita. Yet, moving the title to a portable console seemed like a smart move – these are long games and the social/life sim aspect takes a lot of time, while also being very easy on the pick up and play routine and that’s where a lot of people enjoyed the game even more. Fast forward eight more years and Persona 4 Golden made a surprise showing as a PC port with a few more improvements over the enhanced PS Vita port. And now I’ve finally played the game to the end.

Since Persona series (ever since 3) are so unique in their gameplay, I should start with explaining how they work. As the main character in this game is a student (and unlike P3 PSP port you can only play as a boy here), you’re going to live through an entire year of his life. Going to school, hanging out with friends, helping his uncle and little cousin and… solving unexplained bizarre murder case which has a supernatural explanation. An important aspect of the games, and thankfully the game introduces all of these elements at a good and easy to comprehend pace, are “Social Links” – your connections to all these people around you. Which you “level up” by hanging out with them and helping them during the specific times of day when they are available. You also can and should level up your social skills by performing tasks, reading books or sometimes just as part of game events. All of these things have influence over the story, but the most important gameplay part of them all is in how they influence the jRPG mechanics.

Every “party member” that you get in the game unlocks their “Persona”, an avatar representation of their inner power with special powers. While the main character has an ability to “equip” a huge number of these personas, each of which have their own unique skills, stats, strengths and weaknesses (which is also somewhat similar to how Guardian Force worked in FF8, I suppose). Also these Personas can also be fused together to form new Personas, inheriting skills from the ones that are being fused. All of these elements of the game are directly influenced by the social sim elements, hence the constant balance between the typical dungeon crawling and “normal life”.

It’s a pretty cool idea that most of the time works really well, as the gameplay needs and the story needs complement each other. It wouldn’t work, of course, if the gameplay basics weren’t fun and here’s where Persona 4 is especially good – the combat in the game is genuinely engaging and fun. While the exploration of dungeons, getting treasure chests and entering the fights with the “shadows” is somewhat bland, only helped by cool visual design and awesome soundtrack, the fights themselves are great. They’re almost always about smart use of the strengths and weaknesses of enemies against them. Check out the enemies, figure out what they’re weak to, hit the weakness, get extra hit, knock everyone out, get a special whole team attack in for big damage numbers, adapt to the new situation. It’s so often that jRPGs are either really tedious, because the fights never pose a challenge and feel like time wasters, or are way too complicated with a huge amount of interesting systems and mechanics, where those, who don’t care about the pace of a turn-based combat (like me) just get overwhelmed and tired of each fight. But Persona 4, for the most part, keeps the fights brief enough, while also keeping every one of them engaging.

There are annoying exceptions, of course, and some design decisions are more frustrating than anything, like the fact that if your main character dies the game just ends there. Which can randomly happen quite often at the start of the game, yet by the end it stops being a problem at all. Though, at least the retry options are good (how they work depends on the difficulty setting). The extra dungeon originally added in the Golden version for Vita is more annoying than challenging too. And there are some moments and fights were the difficulty simply spikes really hard. Grinding is part of the game, even if it’s not that severe to get through it and at least, with the fights being fun, it’s not annoying to go through. It just takes up more time than you’d hope it would.

Which is another thing that I didn’t enjoy much – the game is really really long. And while it has enough stories and moments to fill all this time, and quite a lot of them are great and emotional, the story is, overall, a bit too trite. The journey through Persona 4 does make you feel like you’re hanging out with weird friends and when it ends it is sad to see it all end, but… At the same time, there are so many predictable and tired tropes everywhere and quite a few of these characters are just stereotypes that aren’t interesting to explore. Even the main story, that has a potential to be something amazing if only it would take itself seriously enough and avoid the tropes, ends up giving in to the typical save the world ancient beings blah blah elements that are fine in a heroic epic jRPG where Hero Person saves The World from The Evil, but feel out of place in a tale which focuses so much on interacting with people, on personalities and characters. Also the key choices that affect the ending are really badly phrased and don’t fit the “dialogue” system of the game at all. Oh and also some of the jokes and situations are just so eye-rollingly bad – your typical “teenagers do teenager things anime joke #5” stuff that wasn’t funny in 2008 and in 2020 some of it feels tone deaf. I’ve not seen so many “gay panic” jokes since the last time I’ve watched a Michael Bay movie however long ago that has been. And some characters, no matter the situation, are always pervy because haha pervy.

Despite all of that, the great moments, the great gameplay, the great soundtrack and style constantly shine through. Despite being longer than I’d want it to be, I still went back every day to play some more of this game and I won’t be surprised if I do a new game plus playthrough of it some time later. Because Persona 4 Golden is a really fun and unique game. And, I suppose, I did like the mood and the tone of Persona 3 more, at least from what I’ve played of it. Yet, actually playing through 4 was so much more enjoyable. But hey, I wish they’d make an even more updated version of 3 someday on PC anyway. Either way, Persona 4 Golden is a really good game that you should definitely check out, now that it’s out on PC and more people may have access to it. It takes a lot of your time. Not everything about it is great. And you might get tired of the tropes and comic relief that was dated even for 2008 when it first came out. But there’s a really high chance that you will like it and it will, if nothing else, be a memorable experience.

Persona 4 Golden is a unique JRPG with heavy VN elements. Long ago, I emulated the PS2 version which had become one of my favorite JRPGs ever. It was my entry into the series and the only Persona title I had played while waiting for PC ports. If P4G didn't get ported, I would've surely played Persona 3 and 5 on emulator later this year. But now, I will wait again with new hope for Atlus to port the remaining games.

[h1]Story[/h1]

P4G is a Slice of Life/Murder Mystery with supernatural elements. Bizarre murders start occurring in Inaba right after the protagonist moves in. Soon, he learns about the world inside the TV and receives the power of "Persona", the other self. But others have to face and accept their inner dark side... or die.

[i]"I am a shadow...
    The true self..."[/i]

Those who face their true selves unlock Personas and join the ever-growing makeshift high school detective group to find the killer. They steadily get closer to finding the truth of the events. The pacing is slow for all but the last quarter. The plot takes some sharp turns and dives deep into the supernatural. Apprehending the murderer is not the group's last task but it is saving the town- no, the world from deities of japanese mythology.
But they also have a high school life to live. Almost every event you would find in a SoL school anime is in this game. And these events were, for me, the best part of this game. The group made every single one of these events very funny and relaxing.
In contrast, the story related events and S-links are more serious in tone- a complete genre shift from the funny SoL moments. The characters also act headstrong instead of playing a fool.
Overall, the story has many typical JRPG cliches, making the flow mostly predictable- besides a few surprising twists. Supernatural elements were heavily used as plot convenience. The SoL events, S-link events and story related events are completely disjointed. Despite this, after the long journey, the conclusion was emotional and satisfying.

[h1]Characters[/h1]

P4G's cast has a high variety of personalities. In the main cast, we have-

Yu, the Mary Sue protagonist
Yosuke, the one who the entire group makes fun of
Chie, the tomboyish girl who loves meat
Yukiko, the one who laughs at bad jokes
Kanji, the misunderstood delinquent
Rise, the ex-idol who really wants senpai to notice her
Naoto, the genius detective
Teddie, The mascot who also poses as a womanizer
Dojima, the grumpy detective uncle with a soft side
Nanako, the precious imouto who must be protected by all means

We also have many side characters. But they aren't as well developed as the main cast. Even within the main cast, some are more well written than the rest. However, they become an inseparable group of friends with top-tier group dynamics.

[h1]Social Links[/h1]

Mainly one-on-one scenarios where the protagonist helps the characters overcome their internal conflicts and gets closer to them, either as a friend, or romantically. S-Links give you a deeper understanding on the characters. It also unlocks new skills for their personas and gives bonus XP during fusion. However, many irrelevant characters had S-links. Such as- a random middle schooler. They were of lower quality and used as filler content.

[h1]Setting[/h1]

The rural Inaba's distinct feature is the heavy fog after long rainfall. For an RPG game, the exploration is very limited. The number of explorable areas can be counted on one hand. But even if small-scale, it gives a homely vibe.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

The gameplay loop consists of Persona Fusion, Dungeon Crawling, and Free Days.

[u]Persona Fusion[/u]
Personas are deities or demons from various mythologies that aide you in combat. Fusion is the main gimmick of SMT franchise. You can fuse 2 or more Personas into usually a more powerful one and also inherit skills of personas used in the fusion. But for a specific persona, you will end up looking the combos online since there is no clear pattern for the fusions.

[u]Dungeon Crawling[/u]
The weakest aspect of the game is the dungeon design. The 9 dungeons are all designed in the same way, minus the backdrop. Dungeons consist many floors of corridors connected to.. more corridors and sometimes rooms with treasure chests. There is a boss or extra boss at the topmost floor, mini bosses on some floors. The AI of enemies laying in ambush is also dumb. You will only miss a pre-emptive strike due to the weird hitbox. Also, most enemies are reskinned and used across multiple dungeons.
The first 3 dungeons are well balanced. You had to manage your items and SP(used to cast spells). After you run out of SP you call it a day and get out. The next day, you can resume from the farthest floor you reached before. But after the 3rd dungeon, you start amassing a lot of items and money(to recover SP from a fox), and beat dungeons in a single day. A few dungeons later, if you raised Rise's S-link, then you will get free recovery, ailment cure and stat boosts, making resource management pointless.
P4G gets easier with time. The only times I died were on the first dungeon. The main reason it gets easier is due to the ease of leveling up the characters. Go through a dungeon twice without skipping enemies, and you will get over-leveled for later dungeons. The 2nd run of a dungeon is for the extra boss and side quests, and is a cakewalk.
Post battle, "Shuffle Time" randomly triggers where you get to pick from an assortment of cards. These cards include unlocking new personas, raising the stats of your equipped personas, getting more money or xp, recovering HP and SP for entire party, or getting to choose more cards for a penalty to money,xp or items dropped etc.
I liked the element based pokemon-like combat in the early game. Hit an enemy's weakness, or land a critical strike to get 1 more turn. If you down all enemies, you can launch an all-out attack dealing massive damage. But after unlocking Rise as the new navigator, she outright tells you the enemy's resistances, weaknesses, and skillset and also reveals all enemy and treasure chest locations on the floor before you even explore it, killing the surprise factor.
From the 6th Dungeon, you can breeze through almost every normal encounter with light/dark based instant kill spells. These spells become highly accurate and reliable due to plentiful recovery options. But, this playstyle is more repetitive and simplistic compared to the element based combat from earlier.
Boss battles need a different, endurance based approach. Party members are given roles ranging from offense, all-rounder to support. But bosses still don't pose much of a threat since you have many ways to prevent damage and death, especially in late game.

[u]Free Days[/u]
I spent a lot of time on free days because I liked going around the town everyday to talk to all the NPCs to learn about their circumstances and ongoing rumors. But, sometimes there were too many free days without any "gameplay". For me, this gap without a single combat encounter was longer than 10 hours. Of course, you can go into the TV anytime, but then you will miss out S-links.
Besides doing S-links, you can turn in side quests or raise social stats which are required for many objectives. Side quests are filler content. They are either fetch quests or trivia, and the rewards are nothing special.
One of my favorite part of this game is the calendar based progression system. By observing the date change, you can be assured of progress, especially during the subsequently long free days.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

You will like P4G if you are a fan of either VNs, Anime or JRPGs. It is a departure from usual JRPGs- focusing on story and characters a lot more than gameplay. The game is only 20% gameplay, that too, pretty easy except on the highest difficulty. However, the low frequency of combat and high number off days lets you play at your own pace, making it one of the comfiest JRPG ever.

[h1][u]TLDR:[/u][/h1] The maximum word count for reviews does no justice for my thoughts, but here they are:
If you haven't played this game, or any Persona game, or are even remotely interested, you absolutely, 100%, [b]NEED[/b] to play this game. It is a beautiful, indescribable-with-words masterpiece that I proudly proclaim as my favorite game of all time, period. 

[h1]GENRE:[/h1]
Turn-based JRPG dungeon-crawling combined w/ daily life-simulation 

[h1]GAMEPLAY:[/h1]
The game is broken up into calendar days over the course of 1 year. Most days are broken up into different timed sections: [b]Daytime, Afternoon/After School, and Evening[/b]. During each of those sections, you can choose to partake in different activities that are available on that day of the week. 

For the life-sim side, aside from attending school, the gameplay opens up in your choice of what you after school/ when school is closed:

Who do you want to hang out with? (Hanging out with others further develops your bonds (Social Links) with them as you learn about their backstories/struggles)

Which personal stat do you want to grow? (Personal stats (e.g. Knowledge, courage, etc.) are attributes that help you perform other tasks easier, whether it is unlocking new dialogue choices, increasing your performance in the upcoming exam, or allowing you to get past a threshold needed to get further into a social link)

So, what are [b]Personas[/b]? Personas are manifestations of a person's heart; different personalities that one "puts on" in order to face the harsh environment that is life. Personas are you and your party members' tools used for the dungeon-crawling part of the game.

You use Personas to defeat Shadows; Shadows are, as you will hear throughout the game, a person's [i]"true self"[/i]. There's much more to be said about Shadows but I think it's best if you play the game and find out.

Social Links: The more you interact with different characters and build your Social Links, the more experience Personas will receive upon creation and the stronger the Personas you will be able to fuse upon maxing out respective Social Links. 

Dungeons play a key role in gameplay in that as part of the story, you need to enter these unique labyrinths in order to [i]achieve a certain goal by a future deadline[/i], or else the [b]game will end[/b] and force you back a number of weeks to try again. Once the goal has been met, you can return to these dungeons as your choice of activity for a day and grind for experience/money/quest items/material drops etc.
Overall you can expect a lot, and I mean A LOT, of content out of P4G.

[h1]GRAPHICS:[/h1]
The original Persona 4 was released on PlayStation 2, and Persona 4 Golden is a remake/remaster of P4 with new content. So yes, this game does look like a late PS2 game. 
That doesn't mean it looks bad, as actually it looks really good and most things just lack "big" animation. Character/Persona models look great and although they appear kind of stiff in the animation department, they are still able to convey their emotions well like joy, sadness, laughter, anger, etc. The real world settings and dungeons are bright and colorful, and the game's menus and UI are similarly as bright and yellow (P4's main color theme). 

[h1]STORY:[/h1]
*[b]Disclaimer[/b]: If you have never played the game and do decide to play it, this is a friendly reminder to NOT visit any comment section, forum, or wiki page about the game. The core story element of the game is that it is a [b]mystery[/b] why a series of events is occurring. Since this is an 8 (or 12) year old game, some people out there will obviously spoil the mystery. Consider yourself warned.*

You are a city boy who has been transferred to live a year in the countryside town of Inaba. As soon as you start school, a body appears in town and the police begin investigating why something like this has happened in such a peaceful town. Along the way, you somehow discover that you have been given some kind of supernatural power. By using that power, you discover a world never-before-seen where there are hints to the deceased individual's final moments. You soon find out that the individual was not the only victim, as more and more bodies begin to appear in town, all laid out and displayed in bizarre fashions. It turns out that your power, the power of Persona, is a key to the solving of this murder mystery, and that as you pursue the case, you have the potential to save people from becoming the next victims. 

Will you reach out to the truth and figure out the cause of all this?

[h1]STRENGTHS:[/h1]
•Persona 4 Golden has the strongest cast of characters out of any Persona game, let alone any game that I know of. Each member that will eventually become part of your main party, or otherwise referred to as the "[i]Investigation Team[/i]", has such a unique and fun personality, has such realistic background stories/struggles in life, and has such a believable relationship with each other. The side characters are equally as well, if not better, written.

•Phenomenal soundtrack. The music is so catchy, so ear-wormy, so amazing that if you do not end up humming the tracks in your sleep unconsciously, you are lying to yourself.

•There is always something to do and thus, it is hard to get bored. The time management portion of the game is great in that most of the time, you are doing something different every day of the week. 

•Many different Personas to collect and use at your disposal

[h1]WEAKNESSES:[/h1]
•If you've played Persona 5 first and not P4G yet, you will be disappointed by dungeons. The dungeons in P4G are randomly generated as opposed to fixed and detailed like in P5. Thus, the dungeon-crawling experience isn't as strategic and objective-based. Even for those who haven't experienced the P5 dungeons yet, you might feel that the dungeons are just boring hallways with occasional rooms with treasure. Overall, the dungeon-crawling experience in P4G isn't the most exhilarating part of the game.

[b][u]*PC PORT REVIEW*[/u][/b]:
*Disclaimer: I will not talk about Denuvo, [b]not because I support it[/b], but because it did not affect my enjoyment of the game. If you choose to avoid the game based on the introduction of Denuvo, that is entirely your choice and I will not dispute your decision.

•The upscaling resolution and unlocked framerate felt absolutely great. 99% of the game I did not experience a single frame drop, although I have to address the small 1% that is rather noticeable. [i]You will likely experience a small (<1 second) delay that occurs right before a party member's dialogue to initiate an All-Out-Attack and right before Rise chimes in to strengthen an All-Out-Attack[/i]. All throughout my playthrough I was never able to get rid of said delay, but it did not ruin my enjoyment of the game.

•[b]DUAL AUDIO[/b]: Play with either English or Japanese voices (wasn't present in Vita version); a welcome addition

[h1]NUMERIC SCORE (if you care):[/h1]
[b]9.9/10[/b]

Yes, I'm biased and this is my favorite game of all time. Yes, I think more people should definitely play and experience the beauty that is this game. And yes, I hope ATLUS continues to port future Persona games, and even mainline Shin Megami Tensei games, onto the PC platform. Thank you ATLUS for allowing me to play my favorite title again on my PC.

[quote]

[*][h2][b]Story[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Writing[/b] 
You have counted months for solving the mystery. Time will run on the [b]calendar[/b] between sunny, cloudy and rainy days of school lessons, exams, cultural and sports clubs, part-time jobs and quest deadlines. Different weather means different types of activities, [b]time matters[/b]. 
The content is huge, you have [b]different endings[/b] and it needs more than one run to see them all.
◼️ [b]Characters and dialogues[/b] 
Unforgettable characterization of the party, the game plays on the [b]development of the relationship with them[/b]. The party develop throughout the story events and the interactions. You have to speak with them, invite on dates, do activities, reply in the correct manner and way to build up affection. Lines are great and you have [b]different choices[/b] for different outputs.

[*][h2][b]Gameplay[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]How it plays[/b] 
It’s a [b]classic JRPG[/b] that plays between fights and daily life events of the hero, you have total freedom on how to play. Each day you can choose what to do in the afternoon and evening. During those events, your character can develop his skills (understanding, expression, courage, diligence, knowledge), deepen and become closer to characters.
During the main plot mystery event your mission will change and the objective changes to a rescue mission. If you miss the deadline it’s game over. The NPC is in a dungeon full of enemies called [b]shadows[/b], you have to explore, fight and level up to reach the last room and boss. Fights are in turns, you’ll attack, guard, use skill, items and change Personas (if the enemy is strong or weak to a certain one).
◼️ [b]Features[/b] 
The main core of the gameplay is your Personas, that became stronger and competitive only if you have deep relations with the NPC. There is a difference between the [b]character level[/b] and the [b]Persona level[/b] and it can be confusing to newcomers: the player stats scales with the Persona attributes and the gear equipped, the “hero” level changes life and soul point and the number and level of the Personas you can equip. Personas can be obtained by fusion or drop after the fights, the drop session is called shuffling, a minigame of cards where you have to choose between different tarot cards.
Other than that the player has [b]five different stats[/b]: Intelligence, Diligence, Courage, Understanding and Expression. The strength of each stat affects some of the dialogue options that you have in conversations with other characters.
Last but not least the game has a particular feature of [b]asynchronous multiplayer cooperation[/b], the players can help other players in difficulties by actively support them in giving life and soul points to recover.
◼️ [b]Overall difficulty[/b] 
The game can be [b]challenging for newcomers[/b]. Some enemies are immune to skills and they can repel to yourself some types of spells. If you don’t think or use a strategy you will kill yourself.

[*][h2][b]Graphic[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Art Design[/b] 
Colourful, dynamic, anime, visually stunning cut-scenes of the highest quality.
◼️ [b]Characters[/b] 
Kinda low-quality cartoonish 3D model of the NPC, with high-quality visual design during the dialogues or cut-scenes.
◼️ [b]Effects[/b] 
Like the [b]art design[/b], the visual effects are colourful, full of lights and dynamism.

[*][h2][b]Soundtrack and Audio[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]Music, audio effects and voice acting[/b] 
Wonderfully made in [b]Dolby[/b] .The soundtrack is a mix of wonderful [b]JPOP, JROCK, JOPERA[/b] music. [b]English and Japanese dialogue made by professionals[/b], almost everything that is on screen is dubbed. 

[*][h2][b]Extra[/b][/h2]
◼️ [b]DLC[/b] 
The Digital Deluxe version contains the [b]digital artwork[/b] and the [b]digital soundtrack[/b].

Huge because there are [b]different endings[/b], some of them impossible to reach in a single run. The game gives you around ten different activities to choose to do every day. The first walkthrough is a test, you’ll do what you think is good, funny, interesting. You’ll develop your skills and relationship, you’ll power up and fill the Personas compendium. In the [b]NG+[/b] the game starts anew, you’ll bring back the most important things from the first run, you will do what you missed, you’ll develop new skills, you’ll fill up the relation tree, you’ll try to do the Golden ending of the story.

Around [b]80 hours[/b] for the first run (normal), upgrade and double the time counting if you want to see the different endings, achieve all the social links to max or complete the compendium.

[b]50 achievements[/b], more than half achievable during the main quest. A lot of missable or kind of impossible to achieve in the first run.
