[h1][b]Overview: Welcome to Persona[/b][/h1]
[i]Persona 4 Golden[/i] is a game from Atlus which is a turn-based JRPG that contains visual novel elements somewhat reminiscent of Pokémon. To describe for a newcomer to the Persona series is a little difficult but I'll do my best to give a general gist. The general plot follows a high school student in Japan who moves to a new town to live with his uncle. While attending school, your character discovers a series of grisly murders occurring in this little town and discover that an urban supernatural legend known as the 'Midnight Channel' is possibly related to this. With your friends, you set out to find the truth about yourselves and the murders.

[b](+) The Good[/b]
	• Great soundtrack
	• Gameplay is fun, requiring you to manage your social life, school work, after-school jobs, clubs, and hunting down the serial killer with your friends.
	• Game is huge. I'm talking an average of 40 to 80 hours, let alone all the side quests, social links and more that you can complete.
	• Develop meaningful relationships with people all over town
	• Fun anime cutscenes interspersed with the game
	• No need to have played any other games in the series to enjoy this one
	
[b](-) The Bad[/b]
	• The dungeons can be a bit repetitive
	• Grinding for specific items/personas in dungeons can be annoying
	• For a newcomer to the series, it can be slightly overwhelming and confusing on what you can accomplish, especially without a guide
	
[b](-) The Ugly[/b]
	• Honestly, there's nothing I can really point to as 'ugly' in this game. It's damn good.

[h1][b]General Gameplay: A Day in the Life[/b][/h1]
As I explained above, the game is a turn-based JRPG that is similar to Pokémon. You will encounter creatures in a nether realm found inside of a television channel known as the Midnight Channel. These creatures are called personas. Some personas have physical attacks, whilst others can have fire or even ice abilities. Given whatever you're battling, you may need to target a fire persona’s weakness by summoning an ice persona to your side in battle. On top of this, you're joined by a host of friends who have their own personas and abilities that can help swing the battle in your favor. However, the dungeons are only a part of the game.

Beyond this, your character has to manage their daily life. After all, they're a high school student. You can get an after-school job which can improve certain abilities like your courage. On top of this, you need to make sure to study for upcoming exams and sometimes you'll be called out by a teacher and be forced to give them an answer. If you get it right, your knowledge in the game increases.

The biggest thing to keep in mind about Persona 4 Golden is that Social Links are core to develop during your playthrough. You'll meet a host of characters during the game's story and depending on what you choose to say and do, you'll be able to develop closer relationships with your friends and many other people. These relationships are important because they can affect certain story elements and possibly give you bonuses to your combat. However, you do need to dedicate time to hang out with these folks. By hanging out with them, you'll advance the in-game time and miss opportunities to do other things. It's a bit of a tightrope walk, but that's all part of the fun.

[h1][b]Story & World: Flippin' on the Midnight Channel[/b][/h1]
Each Persona game focuses on different ideas, and the main idea behind this game as two general points:

• Investigating a serial murderer with a detective theme
• Confronting one's fears about themselves and understanding their 'truth'

Essentially, this game deals with people lying to themselves. Many people you'll encounter are in denial about the abusive relationships they're in, or perhaps something more intimate. The point is, your character is tasked to find the 'truth' about the world and as you explore this town, you begin to find that truth is something very difficult to discover. This is where personas come in. Personas are physical manifestations of one's inner demon. By refusing to acknowledge your own failings, you're giving power to the persona to protect the hidden truth about yourself. 

And what's the truth? In a non-spoiler way, the truth is that everyone has dark parts about themselves. The question is if whether or not you can accept this part of yourself and learn to be a better person, or run away from the truth and cause destruction to hide this. Persona, for all its anime-weeb design, is a fairly mature examination on what it means to be a human being. Sure, on the surface you're investigating a serial killer who is using a supernatural weapon known as the 'Midnight Channel' to kill their victims. But underneath this, the game is attempting to examine what it means to grow up in a world where nobody is perfect.

[h1][b]Visuals, Sound, & Performance: Shake it like a Polaroid[/b][/h1]
The music is phenomenal. It has pop, rock, and jazz elements from Shoji Meguro. None of it is distracting and while it can be slightly repetitive, it always informs the scene. The voice acting is great and while you're able to play in both Japanese or English, the English VAs are excellent in their delivery.

Visually, it's slightly dated but the game still looks great, especially considering this came out originally in 2008. It's an anime visual style and while it doesn't get wacky very often, it's always fun to watch those scenes.

I personally haven't experienced any bugs or glitches but the game has crashed twice for me. However, this is fairly rare and the only issue I'm hearing from the community is some lag in the cutscenes.

[h1][b]Conclusion: Our Truth[/b][/h1]
Persona 4 Golden isn't a perfect game; for me, I'd still consider Persona 5 Royal to fit that category. Looking back at this game, I can see where Atlus improved on certain mechanics and polished the gameplay in later games, but this doesn't mean this game isn't worth exploring. In fact, if you're at all curious about this game, I'd highly recommend you to check it out. You're bound to discover something truly special, especially if you venture into the Midnight Channel.

I wanted to wait until I finished the game to leave a review, but the closer I get to it, the less I want it to end. [i]Persona 4 Golden[/i] has completely flipped what I thought an RPG could be on its head. After being mindblown by [i]Final Fantasy X[/i], I wasn't sure another RPG would top it. [i]P4G[/i] takes the turn-based combat that I loved in [i]FFX[/i] and just adds an entire second game on top of it.

Rather than sic countless enemies on you in between free-roaming, [i]P4G[/i] allows you to live out your daily routine, going to school with your friends, spending time with them, deepening your relationships, which directly translates to your friends' effectiveness on the battlefield. Not only can you spend time with your friends, but each friend has their own individual story, which progresses as your relationship grows. Completing their stories are rewarding and again help to bolster your companions' power in battle, making it all the worthwhile to get to know everyone. 

Getting to know them is not some boring task either, the characters are nuanced, with understandable feelings, and motivations that feel down-to-earth and relatable. Your friend group spends time together, gets to know each other, and make many memories together. At times it reminds me of [i]Toradora[/i], which is also a very excellent slice-of-life friend group anime. Besides friends, you also have the opportunity to get to know many acquaintances, as well as some of your family members. I will admit it has felt somewhat overwhelming trying to keep up on all of the social bonds, but they are completely optional, however many social bonds will form themselves as the main story progresses.

The main story follows the Protagonist, Yu Narukami (originally unnamed but later given an official name in a spinoff game), a transfer student from the city, as he moves to the small town of Inaba. Shortly after moving, a string of murders take place in the town, and Yu and his friends find themselves right in the middle of it. After accidentally falling through a TV, the friends find themselves in an alternate world, where they are confronted by doppelgangers, who profess their hidden feelings, and the friends must accept their darker sides, to harness that power through a Persona.

The Persona acts as a conduit for the combat abilities of the player character and companions. They learn new moves as they level up, and you can upgrade the moves further. The player character can also collect multiple Personas, and fuse them together to create an entirely different Persona, and it is awesome. Each Persona has an archetype, which directly correlates to an archetype on a social link, which helps to benefit certain Persona types the closer you get with the person of that same archetype.

All this comes together when you enter the TV world, featuring [i]Final Fantasy[/i] style dungeon-crawling battle system, wherein your party of 4 (in total 8 characters, so you'll have to choose who to bring) take turns attacking and using abilities to defeat your enemies. It features type effectiveness, buff and debuff moves, and the game actually gives you the option to allow your NPC companions to execute their own battle commands, as well as give them certain roles such as support or attack. I had all my NPCs set to attack for themselves at first, but as the game progressed I found it infinitely better to just assume control of them and execute the commands myself, but it's nice to have the option there.

A no-brainer 10/10, [i]Persona 4 Golden[/i] has set a new bar for JRPGs for me, and it's a bittersweet feeling. Even before finishing the game, I'm already thinking about how I want to do things differently in my next playthrough. I can't wait to play [i]P4G[/i] again and again.

Edit: I'm amending my review, because it just dawned on me that I completely neglected to mention the soundtrack. This music in this game is next-level, easily the best soundtrack out of every game I've played. The emotion in each song is so clearly depicted, that it instantly informs the player as to the tone of the cutscene, and the battle music is so catchy and energetic that I sometimes take a little too long to take my turn because I'm just listening to the music. It's that good.

Having played both Persona 3 Reload and Persona 5 Royal, I figured it was finally time to experience Persona 4 Golden - especially after the recent reveal of Persona 4 Revival. Right off the bat, what stood out was the UI and battle system. Compared to the slick and stylish interfaces of modern entries, P4G's menus feel jarringly dated (understandable for a game originally released in 2008). Key information - like SP costs, damage types, and skill descriptions - isn’t always clearly presented, and you’re often expected to know what various skills do without much guidance. But nothing that a quick google search couldn't rectify. 

That said, once I adjusted to the 'older' mechanics, I was completely drawn in. Honestly, I went in expecting to be underwhelmed - but I couldn’t have been more wrong. Persona 4 Golden may just be my favourite entry in the franchise.

The story, centered around a string of serial killings in a quiet rural Japanese town, felt unexpectedly gripping. It reminded me of JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Diamond is Unbreakable, but more grounded. What truly surprised me, though, was how attached I became to the cast/companions. By the end, it felt like I had formed a genuine, unbreakable bond with the characters. Each companion's backstory had just the right touch of depth and charm and the same could be said for the various social links in-game as well. 

My one other gripe with this game is the music in general - it just didn’t jive as well with me as a Persona series should. Not my favourite tracks to add to listen to but still okay, I guess. Here’s hoping that P4R does a better remix of the tunes available in-game. 

Some other background information - I played this primary on Steam Deck and it ran flawlessly with no crashes experienced. A full 100% achievement run requires 2 full playthroughs as there’s a hidden superboss to defeat near the end of your second playthrough - so if you intend to 100% this it’s really a significant time investment. If you need a guide for the day-to-day stuff in-game, this is the one I used - https://psnprofiles.com/guide/8564-persona-4-golden-platinum-walkthrough#4-introduction.

Hey, hold on, let me start this properly and say a few words about this beautiful game. 

I want to approach this review by looking at the game entirely on its own, without comparing it with other entries in the Persona series. 

I think what truly defines Persona 4 is undoubtedly its relationship with Jungian psychology. Even calling it a “relationship” feels insufficient. From its mechanics to its narrative structure, the game uses Jungian concepts as actual building blocks. I think that’s exactly why I never got tired of playing it. Traditionally, particularly within mainstream narrative traditions, character attachment is built through dramatic elements such as past trauma, emotional wounds, or visible imperfections that shape the narrative. This is where Persona 4 distinguishes itself from almost every other JRPG. While many games explore character psychology thematically, very few transform it into such a structural principle, which is an incredibly smart design decision. There are many JRPGs that I deeply love, but this series operates on an entirely different level of depth.

It’s probably worth spending a moment on the Jungian system the game is built around. I’m only trying to write a brief summary here, so I’d definitely recommend looking into it further on your own. The system connecting Persona 4 to Jungian psychology is primarily expressed through the archetypes of Persona and Shadow, both of which emerge from what Jung described as the unconscious, the mental space that contains repressed thoughts, hidden desires, and unintegrated aspects of the self. Social relationships belong to the conscious realm, as they are formed through deliberate interaction, choice, and lived experience. However, Jung also identified the collective unconscious, a shared psychological layer common to all humans, structured around archetypes as the inherent capacity to recognize and generate patterns. Because this collective dimension operates like an interconnected network, relationships formed at the conscious level become the space where unconscious patterns are reflected and shared. This is where the game’s Jungian structure truly takes form, allowing Persona 4 to integrate its mechanics, narrative, and design around a single psychological framework.

Still, I think there’s an important limitation to this approach. After characters confront and accept their Shadows, the game often treats this integration as if it’s complete. While later social link scenes indicate that these struggles continue, the game rarely sustains this tension with enough narrative emphasis. Considering that Jungian psychology forms the game’s structural foundation, this consistent optimism feels slightly misleading. Maybe it avoids repetitive misery and keeps the experience uplifting, but it does feel selective. Confronting one’s Shadow doesn’t always lead to moral clarity, and sometimes it can even be dangerous. The game clearly chooses to emphasize the therapeutic side over the darker implications. 

Another aspect I appreciated is how the game handles its mystery. While the twists may not be entirely unpredictable, (aren’t you the sinister one after all? :) the way the game punishes you for following the wrong path is well considered. By placing several decision-based thresholds between the player and the true ending, the game penalizes attitudes such as impatience, overconfidence, and the urge to resolve ambiguity too quickly, thereby shifting failure from an epistemic mistake to an ethical one. When stated this way, the idea can sound somewhat mechanical. However, what sets Persona 4 apart isn’t simply the existence of a true ending, nor the difficulty of reaching it, but the way the game treats the player along that path, and, more importantly, how it makes that process feel. I love the game’s observer stance. This kind of design, where choices genuinely matter in this way and can lead to failure, is unfortunately something many modern games have abandoned. Additionally, by leaving the protagonist largely undefined and offering a wide range of meaningful choices, it creates a strong emergent narrative. The media distortion metaphor is a great touch as well. I don’t think I even need to mention how memorable the characters are or how good the dialogue is.

As for combat, while engaging, it can become repetitive, and the game’s age is most visible here. The system relies more on exploiting enemy weaknesses than on mechanical variety, keeping combat quick and satisfying but less varied in the long run. I mean, it's the classic JRPG formula, especially by older standards. What can you do ... 

Another issue for me is the limited size of the map. I understand and even appreciate the intimacy of the setting, and I’m not expecting an open world or a sandbox experience, but the limited scale of the map can become a bit suffocating over time.

At times, I found myself thinking that Persona 4 could have genuine pedagogical value for players in their late teens or early adulthood. I even felt a quiet envy toward the warmth of its school relationships. Sure, the positivity can feel unrealistic at times, but it's part of its enduring charm, which is interesting, since I’m usually not a big fan of that much positivity. 

Marie wasn’t even part of the original Persona 4, and somehow she ended up being one of my favorite characters. She’s an amazing addition to Golden. Being able to see her inner world through those raw, poetic monologues and witnessing pure emotion in the absence of a fully formed self was genuinely fantastic. Also, WHATEVER HAPPENED WITH MARGARET AT THE END … WHAAAT? This is ... UN-BEAR-ABLE! 
(Of course I didn’t forget you, Naoto. So, when are we opening our detective agency together? Also ... while we’re at it, would you like to go out for dinner tonight?) 

The English dub is surprisingly good. I usually stick to the original audio in games, but this one is absolutely worth choosing. If you’re curious, Persona 4 the Animation is also worth checking out.
